newsitem.title: USA: USDA, FDA seek input for food transport rule.
newsitem.headline: USDA, FDA seek input for food transport rule.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department and the Food and Drug Administration Tuesday said they were seeking public input to craft a new rule on ways to keep perishable foods safe during transportation and storage.
The two agencies plan to publish a joint advance notice of proposed rulemaking this week. Copies of the notice were made available at a roundtable on the issues hosted by USDA.

USDA and FDA said they are considering temperature performance standards, shipper recordkeeping, mandatory HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points)-type systems, voluntary guidelines or combined approaches.
USDA and FDA said they were also mulling not pursuing a regulatory initiative but instead relying on public education and enforcement of current laws and regulations.

They said under a temperature performance standards approach, potentially hazardous foods would be required to be cooled to and maintained at or a below a specific temperature during transportation and storage from the food processing plant to the retail outlet or food service establishment.
The two agencies said the temperatures limits being considered were 41 degrees Fahrenheit and 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

While they noted 45 degrees Fahrenheit would provide a smaller margin of safety, USDA and FDA said it appeared to be an emerging standard for international trade and would be in line with the European Union temperature limit.

On record keeping, the agencies said they were considering requiring carriers of potentially hazardous foods that are shipped in bulk to provide food shippers with records on the last three cargoes and most recent cleaning.
Any HACCP-type system would likely require that potentially hazardous foods be kept at a particular refrigeration or frozen temperature and that it be recorded by thermometer, they said.
The proposed food transport rule is an offshoot of revolutionary meat inspection regulations announced in July that call for scientific testing for sickness-causing bacteria in processing plants.
Each year, there are between 6.5 million and 33 million cases of foodborne illness in the United States.

"Agencies concerned with food safety have devoted relatively few resources to the transportation and storage sectors of the food chain," USDA and FDA said. "There is an absence of data and information about whether adequate and appropriate food safety controls are being employed while food is being transported and stored."
